say.text: Four pairs of look-alikes come next. Commit to each answer first; the feedback then shows the difference between the pair.
Patient A: 58-year-old woman, a tender, irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
Patient B: 45-year-old man, an irreducible, tender groin lump above the inguinal ligament, with a scrotal extension. Which one is more likely already strangulated?

choices.label: Patient B: the inguinal hernia, the commoner groin hernia
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the neck of each sac, not at how many people have each type of hernia.
Yes. The femoral hernia has the highest strangulation risk among groin hernias.
Its neck is narrow and rigid, so a bulky sac can be trapped there.
Tempting: the inguinal hernia is the commonest groin hernia, so it feels like the riskiest one.
Common is about how often, not how likely to strangulate. Which hernia has the narrow neck?
The inguinal hernia is common, but common is not the same as most likely to strangulate.
The femoral hernia carries the highest risk among groin hernias, because its neck is narrow and rigid.
So Patient A, the femoral hernia, is the one most likely already strangulated.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Re-check the rule: risk comes from the neck, not from how common the hernia is.

say.text: What property of a hernia sac explains its risk of strangulation?

choices.label: A narrow, rigid neck with a bulky sac

say.text: Yes. A bulky sac pushed through a narrow, rigid neck can be trapped, and its blood supply cut off.
Tempting: a hernia that many people have sounds like one that often goes wrong.
Ask what happens to the bowel at the neck, not how many people have the hernia.
Frequency tells you how often a hernia occurs, not whether it will strangulate.
Strangulation depends on the neck: a narrow, rigid neck can trap a bulky sac, as in the femoral hernia.
A man has a tender, irreducible femoral swelling. He is passing flatus, with no vomiting and no distension.
His lactate is rising, which points to strangulation. Which lesion fits this picture?

choices.label: Only part of the bowel wall is trapped, without full obstruction
A complete closed loop of bowel sits in the sac
A Meckel's diverticulum lies in the sac
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Does this man show complete obstruction? Count what he is passing and what he is vomiting.
Yes. Richter's hernia traps only part of the bowel wall, so it can strangulate without complete obstruction.
That is why a patient who still passes flatus can have a strangulated hernia and a rising lactate.
Tempting: strangulation sounds like a closed loop, with vomiting and distension. This patient has neither.
Ask whether the whole wall or only part of it is trapped.
A closed loop gives complete obstruction. Richter's hernia is different: it traps only part of the wall, so it can strangulate without complete obstruction.
So a passing patient with no vomiting or distension fits Richter's, the partial-wall lesion.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Richter's is defined by partial wall trapping, not by complete obstruction.

say.text: Tempting: a Meckel's diverticulum is a real hernia content, and it belongs to a famous eponym.
Ask which hernia has that content, and whether the sac here is a partial-wall picture.
A Meckel's diverticulum in the sac is Littre's hernia, a different eponym from Richter's.
Richter's is defined by partial wall trapping, which is the picture in this man.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Keep the eponyms apart: Richter's is the partial wall, Littre's the Meckel's diverticulum.

say.text: Which eponym names a hernia whose sac holds a Meckel's diverticulum?
Yes. Littre's hernia contains a Meckel's diverticulum.
Richter's and Maydl's are different contents: part of the wall, and a W-shaped loop.
Tempting: Richter's is the eponym you just met, and it is the partial-wall one.
Ask which eponym names the content of the sac, not the way it traps the bowel.
Richter's names partial wall trapping, not a content.
Littre's names the hernia that contains a Meckel's diverticulum.
Tempting: Maydl's W-shaped loop is a famous hernia picture, and it is easy to mix up.
Which eponym's content is a diverticulum rather than a loop?
Maydl's hernia contains a W-shaped loop, with the strangulated limb inside the abdomen.
Littre's hernia is the one that contains a Meckel's diverticulum.
Child: 9-month-old, stable, no peritonitis, and ultrasound shows an intussusception.
Adult: 62-year-old, stable, and CT shows an intussusception with a palpable mass. Which pair of managements is right?

choices.label: Child: enema reduction. Adult: resection of the bowel
Child: enema reduction. Adult: enema too, same condition
Child: laparotomy first. Adult: resection of the bowel
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: One diagnosis can carry different causes in a child and an adult. What usually starts it in each?
Yes. A child without peritonitis is reduced by enema under imaging.
An adult's intussusception usually has a tumour as lead point, so it is resected.
Tempting: the same name and the same picture suggest the same treatment.
Ask what usually starts it in a child, and what starts it in an adult.
A child's intussusception is usually idiopathic and ileocolic. An adult's usually has a tumour as lead point.
The cause changes the treatment: the adult lead point is resected, not reduced by enema.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Age changes the cause, and the cause decides the treatment.

say.text: Tempting: a child with an obstruction feels like a theatre case, and surgery seems the safe choice.
What does a stable child with no peritonitis need first?
A stable child without peritonitis is reduced without an operation, by air or saline enema under imaging.
Surgery is for peritonitis, perforation, shock or failed enema reduction.
Why does an adult's intussusception need resection rather than an enema?

choices.label: A pathological lead point, often a tumour, is usual in adults
Adults have the same idiopathic lead point as children

say.text: Yes. An adult's lead point is often a tumour, which is why resection is the answer.
A child's intussusception is usually idiopathic, ileocolic and linked to Peyer's patches.
Tempting: a child's version is idiopathic, so the adult's looks the same.
Ask what the adult's lead point is.
A child's intussusception is usually idiopathic.
An adult's usually has a pathological lead point, often a tumour, and that is the reason for resection.
A 9-month-old is resuscitated and stable, with no peritonitis. Ultrasound confirms an ileocolic intussusception.
What is the best next step?

choices.label: Laparotomy, since surgery is safer in a child

say.text: Yes. Non-operative reduction under imaging is the first step for a stable child without peritonitis.
Theatre is kept for peritonitis, perforation, shock or failed reduction.
Tempting: surgery feels like the careful choice, so it seems the safer answer.
Ask what the criteria for theatre are, and whether this child meets any of them.
Going to theatre by default is the wrong model. A stable child without peritonitis is reduced by enema first.
Surgery is for peritonitis, perforation, shock or failed enema reduction, and none is present here.
A stable 70-year-old man has a sigmoid volvulus on the film, with no peritonitis.
What is the right first step, and what follows it?

choices.label: Endoscopic detorsion with a flatus tube, then elective sigmoid colectomy
Endoscopic detorsion with a flatus tube, then discharge home
Right hemicolectomy, the same for any volvulus
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask two things: is the bowel viable, and what happens to a sigmoid after it is untwisted?
Yes. Sigmoid volvulus without gangrene is detorted endoscopically, with a flatus tube.
It recurs often, so elective sigmoid colectomy follows, usually in the same admission.
Tempting: detorsion untwists the loop, so the job feels finished.
Ask what happens to a sigmoid after it has been untwisted.
Sigmoid volvulus recurs often after detorsion, so elective sigmoid colectomy is advised.
Detorsion is the first step, not the end of care.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Detorsion treats the twist; the colectomy stops it coming back.

say.text: Tempting: a volvulus is a volvulus, so one operation fits all.
Ask which part of the colon this loop is in.
Caecal volvulus is treated by right hemicolectomy, because endoscopic detorsion usually fails.
Sigmoid volvulus without gangrene is detorted first. The site decides the operation.
Which pair is right: the commonest site of colonic volvulus, and the commonest perforation site in closed-loop large bowel obstruction?
Yes. The sigmoid is the commonest site of colonic volvulus.
The caecum perforates most often in closed-loop obstruction, because it has the largest diameter.
Tempting: the caecum is a famous volvulus site, and it also has a famous perforation risk.
Keep the two facts apart: which site is for the twist, and which for the burst?
The sigmoid is the commonest volvulus site, with the caecum next.
The caecum is the commonest perforation site in closed-loop obstruction, by Laplace's law.
Tempting: the sigmoid is the usual volvulus, so it must be the perforation site too.
Ask where the largest diameter sits in the colon.
The caecum has the largest diameter, so it perforates most often in closed-loop obstruction.
The sigmoid is the commonest volvulus site, but that is a different fact.
A stable patient has an obstructing caecal carcinoma. Which operation fits best?

choices.label: Left hemicolectomy, the standard for any colon cancer
Self-expanding metallic stent as definitive treatment
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which side of the colon is this tumour on, and what does the side decide?
Yes. Right-sided obstruction is treated by right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis.
Tempting: one colon cancer, one operation.
Ask which side of the colon this tumour sits on.
The operation follows the side: right-sided cancers get right hemicolectomy.
A left-sided tumour is resected with Hartmann's or a primary anastomosis in a stable patient.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Side first, then the operation.

say.text: Tempting: a stent keeps the bowel open without surgery, so it sounds like the safe answer.
Ask what a stent is for, and on which side it is used.
A self-expanding stent is used for left-sided obstruction, as a bridge to surgery or as palliation.
It is not the definitive treatment for a right-sided tumour.
An adult has small bowel obstruction, and the history says no previous abdominal surgery.
What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: Adhesive bands, the commonest cause in any adult
Crohn's stricture, the common stricture in Indian practice
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Read the history line again. What does 'no previous surgery' rule out?
Yes. In a virgin abdomen adhesions are unlikely, so a surgical cause such as a hernia must be found.
Check all the hernial orifices first.
Tempting: adhesions are the commonest cause of adult small bowel obstruction, so the default feels right.
Read the history line again before you name a cause.
Adhesions are post-operative, so they need a previous operation.
With no previous surgery they are unlikely, and a hernia must be looked for first.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Name the qualifier before the cause: no previous surgery makes adhesions unlikely.

say.text: Tempting: Crohn's is the textbook stricture, so a stricture picture points to it.
Ask which stricture cause is important in India.
Ileocaecal tuberculosis causing stricture is the important stricture cause in India.
Crohn's is not the default stricture here, and in a virgin abdomen a hernia comes first.
A plain film shows a massively dilated loop arising from the pelvis, shaped like a coffee bean. What is the diagnosis?
Yes. A massively dilated pelvic loop with a coffee bean shape is the sigmoid volvulus sign.
A caecal volvulus is a kidney-shaped caecum displaced to the left upper quadrant.
Tempting: both volvulus types make a big loop on a film.
Ask which loop sits in the pelvis and which in the left upper quadrant.
A caecal volvulus is a dilated, kidney-shaped caecum displaced to the left upper quadrant.
The coffee bean belongs to the pelvic sigmoid.
Tempting: intussusception is another obstruction with its own sign on the film.
Ask whether the bowel has twisted on itself or telescoped into itself.
The coffee bean, bent inner tube or omega sign belongs to volvulus.
Intussusception shows a target on ultrasound and a claw on enema.
Which pairing of sign and study is right?

choices.label: Claw sign: contrast enema. Target sign: ultrasound
Claw sign: ultrasound. Target sign: contrast enema
Bird's beak: intussusception on enema. Target: plain film

say.text: Yes. The claw sign is seen on contrast enema, and the target on ultrasound.
The bird's beak belongs to the sigmoid volvulus on contrast enema.
Tempting: the two studies feel interchangeable, since both image the bowel.
Which of the two studies shows a column of contrast in the bowel?
A claw sign is seen on contrast enema, and the target or doughnut on ultrasound.
Swapping the modalities gives the wrong study for each sign.
Tempting: a bird's beak sounds like the shape of an intussusception.
Ask which condition the bird's beak belongs to, and on which study.
The bird's beak is the tapering twist of sigmoid volvulus on contrast enema.
Intussusception shows a claw on enema and a target on ultrasound.
